catalog_quote: Tone is phonemic in Navakat in that there are minimal pairs where the only distinguishing linguistic feature is the tonal distinction. Such pairs display a difference in intonation as well as in pitch, with the vowels with a low tone displaying a falling-rising tonal contour and the vowels with a high or neutral tone exhibiting a level tonal contour. ... làm 'path' lám 'shoe' ... Grammatical morphemes, such as the case markers and conjunctions, do not take tone. Exceptions are some grammatical morphemes in the verb complex: (-)sṍŋ [pst.vis], ʈò [probability], túk [inference]. The tonal distinction is predictable to a large extent. This is consistent with the correlates of the tonal distinctions found in Tibetan in general, i.e., that the main tonal distinction is found only in the first syllable, where plain nasals and liquids tend to co-occur with low tone, but nasals and liquids with …

sources.citation: Saxena, Anju. 2011. The sound system of Nàvakat. Orientalia Suecana 60: 185-192. Uppsala University.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: No stress/accent statement anywhere in the article (a full-text search for stress/accent: stress/accent absent). Tone section is the 2011 original of the 2022 passage: 'Tone is phonemic in Nàvakat ... the main tonal distinction is found only in the first syllable ... The tone of the first vowel determines the tone of the following syllable.' plus one sentence dropped in 2022: 'While the tonal distinction is distinctly audible in lexical items when spoken in isolation, in free speech the tonal differences are not so distinct; instead the main distinctive feature is primarily the tonal contour.' (p. 190).

sources.citation: Sharma, D. D. 1989. Tribal Languages of Himachal Pradesh, Part I (Studies in Tibeto-Himalayan Languages II). Delhi: Mittal. (archive.org CL-CSKHPKV-15657 scanned text)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Part I covers only the Lahul languages (Pattani, Tinani, Gahri, Tod); the Nyamkad sketch is in Part 2 (1992), which is not online. Kept only because it shows Sharma's sketch template includes 'Supra-segmental phonemes' / 'Accent' subsections (e.g. Pattani 2.8.3, Gahri 2.6), so the 1992 Nyamkad sketch very likely contains an explicit accent statement.

sources.citation: Sharma, D. D. 1992. Nyamkad (Nyam-kat). In: Tribal Languages of Himachal Pradesh, Part Two (Studies in Tibeto-Himalayan Languages 3), pp. 97-196. New Delhi: Mittal Publications. ISBN 9788170991021.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Only other description of this languoid (Poo/Namgya dialect, 100 pp.); Sharma's sketches carry a 'Supra-segmental phonemes / Accent' subsection (seen in the 1989 Part I volume), so it is the one place an explicit stress/accent sentence for Khunu-Töt could exist; Saxena 2022 is silent on stress. Would either add a stress note under the tonal coding or confirm silence.
